The constructor should validate that at least one process will be created (or that assigned_shards is non-empty) and raise a clear error otherwise.

findings.body: In `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__`, when `num_processes != 1`, `self.__pool = MultiprocessingPool(num_processes)` is created (line 56). The pool is only closed in `shutdown()` (line 118-120). If the factory is instantiated but `create_with_partitions` raises before the strategy is used, or if the factory object is garbage-collected without `shutdown()` being called (e.g. due to an exception in `get_stream_processor` after factory creation), the multiprocessing pool and its worker processes leak. This is a pre-existing pattern but the new `flusher_processes` parameter increases the surface area. Consider using a context manager or `__del__`/`weakref.finalize` to ensure cleanup, or creating the pool lazily in `create_with_partitions`.

findings.title: SpanFlusher is created with a buffer whose assigned_shards come from partitions, but flusher creates its own per-process buffers — parent buffer's assigned_shards may not match actual Redis shard ownership
findings.body: In `create_with_partitions`, `buffer = SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` (line 67) is passed to both `process_batch` (via partial) and `SpanFlusher`. The SpanFlusher then creates its own per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances (flusher.py line 93). The parent buffer's `assigned_shards` is derived from Kafka partition indices, which is used by `process_spans` to route spans to Redis shards. The flusher's per-process buffers use the same shard list. However, if `SpansBuffer` internally maps shard indices to Redis cluster nodes/instances, having multiple buffer instances (parent + N children) each potentially opening their own Redis connections to the same shards is wasteful and may cause connection storms. More critically, if the shard-to-Redis-node mapping is not purely a function of shard index (e.g. depends on consistent hashing of the full shard set), the child buffers with partial shard lists may route to different Redis nodes than the parent buffer, causing spans to be written to one node and flushed from another — resulting in lost segments. The buffer implementation must guarantee that a subset of shards maps to the same Redis instances regardless of which buffer object performs the operation.

findings.title: test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify that flushing actually works with shared processes
findings.body: The new test `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts that `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that shards are distributed across the process map. It never submits any spans, never advances the drift, and never verifies that segments are actually flushed to `messages`. With `produce_to_pipe` set, the flusher runs in threads, but the test calls `step.join()` immediately without any `submit()` or `poll()` calls. This means the test would pass even if the flusher processes/threads were completely broken (e.g. crashed on startup, never flushed anything). The test should submit at least one span, advance the drift, poll, and assert that a message was produced, to verify that the multi-process flusher actually functions with shared shards.

findings.title: test_basic uses a fixed 0.1s sleep to wait for flusher thread, which is flaky
findings.body: In `test_basic`, after setting `fac._flusher.current_drift.value = 9000`, the test calls `step.poll()` then `time.sleep(0.1)` (line 62) to "give flusher threads time to process". This is a race: 0.1 seconds may not be enough on a loaded CI machine, causing the test to fail intermittently when `step.join()` is called before the flusher thread has produced the message. The test should poll in a loop with a timeout (e.g. wait up to 5 seconds for `messages` to be non-empty) rather than relying on a fixed sleep. The `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top also patches `time.sleep` globally, but the explicit `time.sleep(0.1)` call at line 62 uses the real `time.sleep` because it was imported as `import time` and the monkeypatch patches the `time` module's `sleep` attribute — actually this does patch it, making the sleep a no-op, which means the test relies entirely on `step.poll()` and `step.join()` timing, making the race even worse. The test needs a proper wait condition.

findings.title: test_backpressure only tests single-shard case; multi-process backpressure aggregation is untested
findings.body: The updated `test_backpressure` creates `SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=list(range(1)))` — a single shard — so `num_processes` is 1 and `process_backpressure_since` has a single entry. The assertion `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` trivially passes with one element. The new multi-process backpressure logic in `submit()` (iterating `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` and raising `MessageRejected` if ANY process is in backpressure) is not tested with multiple processes/shards. A test with multiple shards and multiple processes should verify that backpressure from one process triggers `MessageRejected` for the whole consumer, and that backpressure is correctly tracked per-process.

findings.title: --flusher-processes CLI option has no validation for negative or zero values
findings.body: The new `--flusher-processes` click option (lines 432-437) is defined with `type=int, default=1` but has no validation callback. A user can pass `--flusher-processes 0` or `--flusher-processes -5`. A value of 0 will, due to the `or` fallback in `SpanFlusher.__init__` (flusher.py line 51), silently become `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` — not what the user asked for. A negative value will cause `min(negative, len(shards))` to be negative, making `num_processes` negative, which will cause `range(self.num_processes)` to be empty and `i % self.num_processes` to raise `ZeroDivisionError` or produce nonsensical behavior. The option should use `click.IntRange(min=1)` or a callback to reject non-positive values.

findings.title: Restart counter check uses `>` instead of `>=`, allowing MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS+1 restarts
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the check `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` (line 247) raises RuntimeError only when restarts exceed 10. This means the process can be restarted 11 times (restarts 0→1→...→10→11, and the check fires when restarts==11, i.e. after 11 restarts have already happened). The intent of `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` is presumably to give up after 10 restart attempts. Using `>=` would raise after the 10th restart attempt (when `process_restarts` reaches 10). With `>`, the consumer tolerates one more restart than intended, which could delay crash detection by one cycle. This is a minor off-by-one but could matter for alerting thresholds.

findings.title: Health check for 'hang' doesn't account for processes that are alive but stuck in produce()
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the hang detection (lines 231-236) checks if `int(time.time()) - self.process_healthy_since[process_index].value > max_unhealthy_seconds`. `healthy_since` is updated in `main()` at line 179, which runs at the top of each loop iteration. However, if the process is stuck inside `produce()` (line 197) or `future.result()` (line 200-201) — e.g. Kafka is slow or down — `healthy_since` won't be updated, and the hang will eventually be detected. But the check only runs when `submit()` is called on the main thread. If no messages are being submitted (idle consumer), `_ensure_processes_alive` is never called, and a hung flusher process won't be detected until new messages arrive. The `poll()` method (line 215-216) only calls `self.next_step.poll()` and does not call `_ensure_processes_alive()`. Health checks should also run in `poll()` to detect hung processes during idle periods.
